title: Optimizing Data for AI Chatbots
html:
Optimizing Data for AI Chatbots

We all know that AI is rapidly changing how people interact with information. And, whether we like it or not, AI chatbots will likely become the new “first reader” of the data we publish. For the humanitarian sector it means that:

  • Donors will increasingly use AI to check funding patterns.
  • Researchers will feed datasets into chatbots to explore trends.
  • Journalists will run quick analyses to verify claims.
  • Students and volunteers will  rely on AI to understand humanitarian operations.
  • And inside organizations, staff will use these tools to speed up analysis and decision‑making.

This shift creates a change in who interacts with our data. In the past, data was generally handled by experts - specialists who knew the quirks of a specific dataset and could manually correct for “bad data” as they worked. Today, we are seeing the rise of the “Initiator”, a concept explained to me by Jerri Husch as non-data experts who use AI to jump straight into exploration. Since they do not have years of experience with the underlying spreadsheets, they might not realize when a merged cell or a cryptic abbreviation has led the AI to a false conclusion. 

So what’s the issue with AI reading humanitarian data? Because most publicly available humanitarian datasets, however well‑intentioned, are not structured in ways that AI systems can reliably interpret. Research showed that even the most advanced AI models can experience up to a 59% drop in accuracy when confronted with real‑world humanitarian datasets that contain common issues: merged cells, missing values, inconsistent formatting, unclear column names, extra rows, or oversized files. This means that AI-generated insights can easily become flawed: incorrect totals, missing rows, invented numbers, wrong trends, or misleading conclusions. Bad data can no longer be overlooked; it must be fixed at the source.

Thus, the question becomes: What can a data provider do to help increase the chances that AI interprets their data correctly? Together with Ralfs Rudzitis, we set out to explore this question with an overall objective of developing practical recommendations for those who provide downloadable* data. 

The good news is that the solutions are practical, accessible, and within reach for organizations of any size. They are:

  1. Keep your data clean and simple. Delete unnecessary columns and rows. Avoid merged cells. Ensure column names are in the first row. Use one table per sheet.
  2. Use clear, human‑readable column names. Use full words (e.g., Donor_Organization, not DonOrg). Avoid cryptic abbreviations or codes unless documented. Use underscores or spaces, not dots.
  3. Provide context and metadata. If you provide an Excel file, consider adding a second sheet that: explains every column, clarifies abbreviations, provides basic guidance on how the dataset should be read.
  4. Favor “wide” rather than “long” datasets. AI chatbots are surprisingly better with more columns and fewer rows than the opposite. If possible, structure or aggregate data accordingly to increase accuracy.
  5. Include instructions in the dataset or accompanying page. Even a short paragraph can prevent major misinterpretations. What the dataset represents. What limitations exist. What filters or assumptions should (or should not) be applied. Which values indicate missing or invalid data.

For more details and a self-assessment checklist, see the full report Optimizing Data for AI Chatbots 2026

Why this matters for the humanitarian sector

Humanitarian data is a public good. We publish it so that people can use it to make better decisions, generate insights, and strengthen accountability. And now, non-experts are increasingly augmented with AI chatbots. If AI is going to analyze our data, and it will, then we must prepare our data for AI. This is not a luxury, but a modern data responsibility.

The good news is that it does not require new budgets, new software or new teams. Just better habits.

Andrej

* While our findings focused on downloadable data and not (well structured) APIs or MCP servers, it is highly probable that many of the recommendations may still apply.
